questions.stem: A nurse on a step-down unit transferred a client to the ICU two days ago. Today she wonders whether he survived his emergency surgery. Which statement by the nurse shows correct understanding of confidentiality?
options: “I can check his chart as long as I don’t share what I read.”
“I won’t open his chart, because I’m no longer caring for him.”
“I cared for him before, so I still have a right to his chart.”
“I’ll just look at his vital signs instead of his whole chart.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Looking without a work reason is a breach even if the nurse tells no one.
Correct. Without a current work reason, opening his chart would be an unauthorized access.
Incorrect. Past care does not give ongoing access once the nurse’s role has ended.
Incorrect. Looking at any part of the record without a work reason is still a breach.
questions.rationale: Confidentiality applies to obtaining information: nurses may access only what they need to care for their current clients. Once this client was transferred, the nurse no longer has a work reason to open his record, even with caring intentions. Audit logs record every access, and curiosity is not a valid reason. Believing that past care gives ongoing access is the common trap, because the right to look ends when the care role ends.
questions.takeaway: Access a chart only while you have a current work reason; caring curiosity is not one.
questions.hintContent: Is the nurse still involved in this client’s care?
questions.hintStrategy: For “correct understanding” items, eliminate statements that justify access by intent or by how little is viewed.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · HIPAA, Privacy & Confidentiality · Unit 7 slide 24

questions.stem: A caller says she is a pharmacist at a community pharmacy and asks the nurse to confirm the oxycodone prescription a client received at discharge this morning. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Confirm the prescription, since pharmacists are part of the care team
Refuse, because prescriptions cannot be discussed over the phone
Call the pharmacy back at its listed number before discussing it
Ask the caller for the client’s birth date to verify the request
optionRationales: Incorrect. A dispensing pharmacist may receive this information, but only after the caller’s identity is verified.
Incorrect. Sharing with a verified pharmacist filling the prescription is permitted for treatment.
Correct. Calling back the listed number verifies the caller is a real pharmacist before PHI is shared.
Incorrect. A person posing as a pharmacist may already know the birth date, so this does not prove identity.
questions.rationale: Sharing PHI with providers involved in care, including the pharmacist filling a prescription, is permitted. However, the nurse must first verify that the caller really is who she says, especially for a controlled substance that can be diverted. Calling the pharmacy back at its published number is a reliable way to confirm identity. Asking for the client’s birth date is tempting because it is a standard identifier, but it confirms the client, not the caller.
questions.takeaway: Verify a caller’s identity independently before sharing PHI, even with someone who claims a care role.
questions.hintContent: Which option confirms who the caller is, not who the client is?
questions.hintStrategy: For phone-request items, choose the step that verifies identity through an independent source before any disclosure.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · HIPAA, Privacy & Confidentiality · Unit 7 slide 24

questions.stem: During one shift, an emergency department nurse cares for several clients. Which disclosures are permitted without the client’s written authorization? Select all that apply.
options: Confirming to a reporter that a named bus crash victim was admitted
Faxing a client’s drug screen results to his employer’s HR office
Reporting suspected neglect of a 7-year-old to child protective services
Reporting a confirmed case of measles to the local health department
Calling a consulting cardiologist about a client’s abnormal ECG
Telling the coworker who drove a client in that she had a miscarriage
optionRationales: Incorrect. Confirming a named person’s admission to the media discloses PHI; media requests go to public relations.
Incorrect. Employers need the client’s written authorization to receive test results.
Correct. Reporting suspected child neglect is required by law and is a permitted disclosure.
Correct. Measles is a reportable disease, and public health reports are required by law.
Correct. Sharing with a provider involved in care is permitted for treatment.
Incorrect. The coworker is not involved in care and has no right to this PHI without permission.
questions.rationale: PHI may be shared without written authorization for treatment, payment, and health care operations, and when a law requires a report. Reports of suspected child abuse or neglect and reportable diseases such as measles are legal exceptions, not breaches of confidentiality. Consulting another provider about a client’s care is treatment. The coworker who drove the client is tempting because she is helping, but driving someone in does not make her part of the care team or entitle her to sensitive information.
questions.takeaway: Treatment sharing and reports required by law are permitted disclosures; others need client permission.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each disclosure is for treatment or is required by law.
questions.hintStrategy: In disclosure SATA items, identify the legal reason for each share; no reason means no share.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · HIPAA, Privacy & Confidentiality · Unit 7 slide 24

questions.stem: An assistive personnel (AP) asks the nurse, “Is the man in room 12 the one with AIDS? I want to know before I give him his bath.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Yes, so please wear a gown and double gloves when you give him his bath.”
“I can’t share that, but wear a gown and double gloves to be safe.”
“Use standard precautions for all clients; his diagnosis doesn’t change that.”
“That information is private, and only his assigned nurses may know it.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This discloses a diagnosis the AP does not need and adds precautions not required for bloodborne infections.
Incorrect. It withholds the diagnosis, but advising extra gear implies the answer and reinforces the myth that precautions depend on a known diagnosis.
Correct. Standard precautions protect the AP, and the diagnosis is not part of the minimum needed for a bath.
Incorrect. It protects the diagnosis, but it does not tell the AP how to stay safe. Teaching standard precautions answers the real concern behind the question.
questions.rationale: The minimum necessary rule means staff receive only the PHI needed for their task. For a bath, the AP needs to know about mobility, skin concerns, and safety needs, not the client’s HIV status. Standard precautions are used with every client because infection status is often unknown, so the diagnosis does not change how the AP protects herself. Answering “yes” and adding extra gear is tempting because it seems protective, but it discloses PHI and reinforces the false idea that precautions depend on a known diagnosis.
questions.takeaway: Give team members only what their task needs, and teach standard precautions for every client.
questions.hintContent: What does the AP need to know to give a safe bath?
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation items, choose the response that is both private and teaches the staff member something useful.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · HIPAA, Privacy & Confidentiality · Unit 7 slide 24
